AI-Assisted Verification Coursebook
Module 2 — Smart Skepticism, Ethics, and Human-in-the-Loop (HITL)
As AI systems become increasingly integrated into journalism and digital communication, journalists must learn not only how to use AI tools, but also how to question, evaluate, and supervise them critically.

This module explores the ethical, editorial, and professional challenges associated with AI-assisted verification and automated information systems. Learners examine issues such as AI hallucinations, algorithmic bias, transparency, accountability, privacy, and responsible newsroom decision-making while applying the human-in-the-loop (HITL) approach to verification workflows.

The module emphasizes that AI-generated outputs should never be accepted uncritically. Instead, journalists must maintain editorial judgment, ethical responsibility, and human oversight throughout the verification process.
1
Hallucinated Source Detection Activity
In this activity, participants are presented with a text passage generated by an AI tool, containing a mix of real and fabricated sources. The user is asked to identify which source is a hallucination (i.e., does not exist in reality). When the correct choice is made, an explanation is provided on how AI hallucinations occur and why verification is required.
Learning outcome: The ability to recognise fabricated sources in AI outputs and critically evaluate them.

2
Bias Recognition Scenarios
he user is presented with two realistic scenarios that may arise in journalism and verification (e.g., algorithmic bias in facial recognition, English‑biased datasets ignoring local news). For each scenario, the user is asked what type of bias is involved (algorithmic bias, coverage bias, etc.). After making a choice, the correct answer and an explanation are displayed.
Learning outcome: Distinguishing different types of algorithmic bias and understanding their impact on news workflows.
Bias Recognition | Module 2

🎭 Bias Recognition Scenarios

AI systems can support journalism workflows, but they can also introduce bias, inaccuracies, hallucinations, and ethical risks when used without critical oversight.

This module helps learners develop the skepticism, ethical awareness, and editorial responsibility necessary to work with AI systems responsibly in modern digital journalism environments.
3
Ethical Newsroom Simulations
The user is forced to make decisions based on two ethical dilemmas:
  • Privacy vs public interest: An AI flags a minor’s protest location as “newsworthy” based on engagement metrics.
  • Accountability for AI errors: An AI summarisation tool misquotes a politician; the error goes viral.
The user chooses one of three options, after which the best ethical practice and the action aligned with HITL principles are explained.
Learning outcome: Ethical decision‑making and a sense of responsibility in AI‑assisted journalism.
Ethical Newsroom Simulations | Module 2

⚖️ Ethical Newsroom Simulations

Two realistic ethical dilemmas. Choose the best course of action based on HITL principles.
4
Transparency Checklist Exercises
The user is given a checklist of actions a newsroom should take to ensure transparency when using AI. They must select the correct items from a list of five (e.g., “disclose when AI tools are used”, “explain the limitations of the AI model to the audience”). After submitting, they receive a transparency score and feedback on missing or incorrect items.
Learning outcome: Understanding what elements constitute AI transparency in journalism and why they are critical for audience trust.
Transparency Checklist | Module 2

📋 Transparency Checklist

Which of these actions should a newsroom take to ensure transparency when using AI in verification? (Select all that apply)

5
Human‑in‑the‑Loop Decision Tasks
The user is presented with two tasks:
  • Despite a high AI confidence score: An AI says a video is 94% likely to be a deepfake, but manual analysis shows no obvious artifacts.
  • Automated transcription error: An AI writes a wrong name, creating a risk of defamation.
For each task, the user chooses between blindly trusting the AI, completely rejecting it, or following HITL principles by conducting in‑depth verification with human intervention. After the choice, the correct HITL approach is explained.
Learning outcome: Internalising the HITL principle – AI is an assistant, while final decisions and responsibility remain with humans.
HITL Decision Tasks | Module 2

🔄 Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) Decision Tasks

Apply the HITL principle: AI assists, humans decide. Choose the correct action for each scenario.
6
Reflection‑based Mini Quizzes
To reinforce the key concepts of Module 2, three multiple‑choice or short‑answer reflection questions are offered. The questions focus on automation bias, AI hallucinations, algorithmic transparency, and the necessity of human oversight. After the user selects their answers, a “Submit Answers” button shows the total score and personalised feedback on which topics may need further review.
Learning outcome: Self‑assessment of the knowledge acquired from the module and identification of areas for improvement.
Reflection Mini Quizzes | Module 2

💭 Reflection Mini Quizzes

After completing this module, learners will develop a critical and ethically informed approach to AI-assisted verification, combining responsible AI use with human editorial judgment and professional verification culture.
